article.title: Reject “Electoralism.” Embrace Socialist Electoral Strategy.
article.author: Elliot Lewis
article.content: In elections this year, 169 (and counting) candidates or ballot initiatives endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) nationally or by its chapters succeeded at city, state, and federal levels. DSA member Zohran Mamdani is the mayor of the largest city in the country, and it seems increasingly possible that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will run for president of the United States in 2028. These exciting developments raise the question of the role of elections in the socialist project. Today some on the Left refer to socialists running for office as “electoralism.” But that term has a specific historical meaning, which much of the radical left has long viewed with disdain. It’s worth getting clear on what distinguishes electoralism in that sense from a transformative democratic socialist electoral strategy like the one many in DSA are trying to work toward today. Unlike anarchist or syndicalist approaches to organizing, which view militancy outside of the state as the sole mechanism for bringing about social change, both electoralist and democratic socialist electoral strategies see contesting elections as an important tool for helping bring about socialism. But while electoralism focuses exclusively on winning elections and making change through policy measures, a democratic socialist strategy understands elections and socialist governance as one important means among others of achieving reforms and facilitating the organization of the working class into an agent capable of transforming society. Electoralism and Social Democracy Electoralism has existed nearly as long as the socialist movement itself. In Evolutionary Socialism , published in 1899, German socialist Eduard Bernstein argued that capitalism could be gradually overcome through a peaceful electoral path and piecemeal legislative reform. In the early twentieth century, social democratic parties across Western Europe seemingly began making good on this vision, winning state power through elections and attempting to enact pro-worker reforms. Though most early socialists did not think of themselves as “electoralists” and understood the importance of organizing outside the state, particularly in the workplace, over time social democratic strategy focused more and more on winning elections and parliamentary power. Social democrats eventually became electoralists in practice, if not in name. When social democratic parties were on the rise in the early and mid-twentieth century, the industrial working class was increasingly joining unions and engaging in mass strikes, giving the parties significant political leverage . This combination of power inside and outside the state allowed socialists to pass significant policy measures that improved the lives of millions, like universal health care, vacation for all, and expansive labor rights. The growing power of the working class outside of the state at the time also helped conceal the problems that the social democrats’ increasingly electorally focused strategy would eventually face. As time wore on, however, social democrats in government found themselves constrained to merely managing capitalist economies — whose center of power lay not in the state but in the hands of private capital owners who could withhold or offshore their investments if they felt sufficiently threatened, causing economic turbulence and eventually leading to socialist electoral defeat. Many social democratic parties began abandoning the end goal of bringing about socialism entirely, focusing on achieving reforms within capitalism instead. The problem was worsened by the fact that the labor movement, social democrats’ traditional base of power, slowly ossified and came to represent an ever smaller proportion of the working class. In periods of economic stagnation, as in the 1970s and ’80s, this dynamic led socialist governments such as François Mitterrand’s in France to impose austerity measures in an attempt to appease capital and maintain growth. But this too ultimately undermined their popularity and brought about their electoral ousting. In recent decades, declining union density has accelerated this dynamic, leading desperate left-wing parties to try to cobble together broader populist coalitions in order to win a plurality of votes. But these parties have then found that they lacked the organized power outside of the state to overcome the leverage of capital once they entered government, as we saw with the collapse of Podemos in Spain and Syriza in Greece. The core reason that postwar social democratic parties failed, then, was not that party leaders betrayed their base, but that the structural economic conditions imposed by capitalist social relations give owners of capital significant power over the state, limiting socialists’ ability to implement policy reforms absent independent bases of popular power. Social democrats often took this structural imbalance of power between capital and workers outside of the state as an unchangeable given, adopting an electoralist approach at the expense of reconstituting working-class organization. An Alternative to Electoralism: a Democratic Socialist Electoral Strategy Observing the crisis of social democracy in the 1970s, the Marxist philosopher Nicos Poulantzas theorized a democratic socialist electoral strategy as an alternative to both Leninist insurrectionism and social democratic electoralism. For Poulantzas, the state was a terrain of struggle that could be used by socialists to enact transformative change, but only if it was used to help build independent working-class power that would solidify this change and shift power from capital to workers. Adam Przeworski developed this idea further with the concept of class formation. Przeworski argued that whether proletarians act on their class interests rather than their many other interests (as, e.g., homeowners or college graduates or Catholics) depends on whether a political struggle brings class interests to the fore. This struggle is not just about changing people’s ideas but also about changing the world to materially align people around their shared class interests. For example, socialists in Sweden significantly reduced the wage gap between different types of workers through their “ solidaristic wage policy,” thereby not only raising the floor for the lowest-paid workers and reshaping the economy around more efficient industries but also leveling material differences between different segments of the working class. Today the biggest challenge American socialists face is a politically fragmented working class and a weak labor movement decimated by decades of neoliberal attacks. A democratic socialist electoral strategy aims to use electoral campaigns and socialist governance to slowly rebuild working-class consciousness and organization in order to reconstitute the popular power needed to transform society. Such a strategy situates those efforts within a broader approach alongside equally necessary grassroots organizing in workplaces and neighborhoods. Using Elections to Agitate and Organize What does such an electoral strategy, as opposed to mere “electoralism,” look like in practice? For one thing, socialists can use campaign communications to clarify the lines of class struggle. Bernie Sanders’s presidential campaigns exemplified this approach to messaging, with his “Not Me, Us” language, his calls for political revolution, and his frequent finger-pointing at the billionaires who benefit from our current class society. Once in office, socialists can continue to raise people’s political awareness by pointing out when capital stands in the way of much-needed reform or is otherwise harming the interests of working people. Mayor Mamdani’s “Rental Ripoff Hearings” are an excellent example of this type of us-versus-them line drawing, as are Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s frequent viral denunciations of corporate greed in her House speeches. Electoral campaigns can also be used to build socialist organization, as DSA has done in recent years by building out volunteer-led organizing efforts that engage thousands of volunteers in outreach to the broader working class — not only reaching more voters but also developing activists who may continue organizing in the socialist movement for years to come. Socialists in office can go beyond changing peoples’ ideas too: they can use their political power to make it easier for workers, renters, and consumers to build collective organization, thereby increasing the potential power of the socialist movement in the long run. One way to facilitate working-class organization is to use the power of the state to bolster organizing directly, for example by helping tenants and workers organize through public offices dedicated to the task, as the Mamdani administration has begun to do with its Office of Tenant Protection and Office of Worker Power. When socialists have greater political power, they can also pass legislation that directly empowers organizing, like reforming labor law to make it easier to unionize or establishing enforceable collective bargaining rights for tenant unions. With enough power, socialists can start to change the broader structures of the economy to shift power from capital to the working class — for instance, by nationalizing key industries. Even smaller reforms along the way, such as rent freezes and reducing transit costs, can grow support for the socialist project while redistributing resources. Finally, a democratic socialist electoral strategy recognizes the limited power of elections alone on the road to socialism. While winning elections and passing legislation are an essential part of building political power, democratic socialists must equally prioritize building people power beyond elections through union, tenant, and social movement organizing. Recognizing what elections can’t do is as important as understanding how we can best use them to build power. Most socialists in the United States today believe in the importance of contesting elections and taking state power to make change. But as the movement grows, socialists should avoid the pitfalls of a pure-and-simple electoralism that focuses on electing candidates and getting policy passed to the exclusion of all else. Such an approach sets the movement up for disaster when capital brings its leverage to bear in the context of a disorganized working class. We should instead be pursuing a democratic socialist electoral strategy, using campaigns and elected office alongside grassroots organizing to help rebuild the independent bases of working-class power that will be needed to achieve socialism in the long run.
